TAB-ADVANCED-EMAIL-VALIDATION.ALLOW_SQUARE_BRACKETS_IN_A_TEXT: Allow Square Brackets In a Text
TAB-ADVANCED-EMAIL-VALIDATION.SKIP_EMAIL_VALIDATION: Skip Email Address Validation for the Following Email Addresses

INNER-HTML.ALLOW_QUOTED_IDENTIFIERS: these criteria states that as per RFC 2822, quoted identifiers are allowed (using quotes and angle brackets around the raw address), e.g.: "John Smith" <john.smith@somewhere.com> The RFC says this is a valid mailbox. If you don't want to allow this, because for example, you only want users to enter a raw address (john.smith@somewhere.com - no quotes or angle brackets), then don't include these criteria. It is recommended to keep these criteria.
INNER-HTML.ALLOW_PARENS_IN_LOCALPART: these criteria allows as per RFC 2822 ")" or "(" to appear in quoted versions of the localpart (they are never allowed in unquoted versions) You can disallow it, but better to include these criteria.If these criteria is not included, it will prevent such addresses from being valid, even though they are: "bob(hi)smith"@test.com. It is recommended to keep these criteria.
INNER-HTML.ALLOW_DOMAIN_LITERALS: these criteria changes the behavior of the domain parsing. If included, the parser will allow 2822 domains, which include single-level domains (e.g. bob@localhost) as well as domain literals, e.g.: someone@[192.168.1.100] or john.doe@[23:33:A2:22:16:1F] or me@[mycomputer] The RFC says these are valid email addresses, but most people don't like allowing them. If you don't want to allow them, and only want to allow valid domain names (RFC 1035, x.y.z.com, etc), and specifically only those with at least two levels ("example.com"), then don't include these criteria.
INNER-HTML.ALLOW_DOT_IN_A_TEXT: these criteria allows "." to appear in a text (note: only a text which appears in the 2822 "name-addr" part of the address, not the other instances) The addresses: Kayaks.org <kayaks@kayaks.org> Bob K. Smith<bobksmith@bob.net> ...are not valid. They should be: "Kayaks.org" <kayaks@kayaks.org> "Bob K. Smith" <bobksmith@bob.net> If these criteria is not included, the parser will act per 2822 and will require the quotes; if included, it will allow the use of "." without quotes.
INNER-HTML.ALLOW_SQUARE_BRACKETS_IN_A_TEXT: these criteria allows "[" or "]" to appear in a text. Not very useful, maybe, but there it is. The address: [Kayaks] <kayaks@kayaks.org> ...is not valid. It should be: "[Kayaks]" <kayaks@kayaks.org> If these criteria is not included, the parser will act per 2822 and will require the quotes; if included, it will allow them to be missing. One real-world example seen: Bob Smith [mailto:bsmith@gmail.com] Use at your own risk. There may be some issue with enabling this feature in conjunction with Allow Domain Literals. If the Allow Domain Literals criteria is not included, it should be pretty safe. Whether it's useful, that's up to you.

INNER-HTML.ABOUT:
A list of external tools which bring additional value when used together with DataPallas


A good chunk of the below tools can be easily installed and/or uninstalled using Chocolatey, a very good package manager for Windows. All the below commands should be executed by first starting a DOS/Powershell command prompt and then by typing the respective commands inside the DOS/Windows Powershell command prompt.

It is recommended to start the DOS/Powershell command prompt using Windows Start button -> Search for DOS/Powershell -> Right mouse click and then select "Run as administrator"
INNER-HTML.NOTEPADPLUSPLUS: is a free (as in “free speech” and also as in “free beer”) source code editor and Notepad replacement. Notepad++ is useful when editing DataPallas configuration files and scripts.
INNER-HTML.VSCODE: is a code editor redefined and optimized for building and debugging modern applications.
INNER-HTML.WINMERGE: is an Open Source differencing and merging tool for Windows. WinMerge can compare both folders and files, presenting differences in a visual text format that is easy to understand and handle. WinMerge can be used for comparing DataPallas configuration files and scripts.
INNER-HTML.DOCKER-DESKTOP: a very good containerization software. Docker is required for running (some) DataPallas extra packages.
INNER-HTML.MAVEN: is a build automation and dependency management tool for Java projects.
INNER-HTML.DUCKDB: is a single, dependency-free executable that lets you run SQL queries and manage DuckDB database files directly from the terminal.

This sample shows how to generate individualized Student Profile PDF files using an SQL datasource (the Sample Northwind SQLite database).

It also demonstrates how to use (Apache) FOP to produce "pixel perfect" PDF reports suitable for high-quality printing and precise layout control.

This sample demonstrates how to generate individualized Customer Statement HTML documents from a SQL datasource (the Sample Northwind SQLite database). The report runs a SQL query that returns one row per customer and the engine performs a mail-merge to create one HTML file per customer (file name uses the burst token, e.g. ALFKI.html).

Use this example to learn how to configure the SQL datasource (database connection code and query), configure an HTML template for rendering statements, and enable per-customer output. Ideal for producing customer-facing statements, archival HTML exports or per-customer delivery via email or cloud upload.

This sample shows how to generate a single consolidated Customer Sales Summary workbook (.xlsx) from a SQL datasource (the Sample Northwind SQLite database).

The report runs an SQL query to aggregate sales by customer and writes the result to one output Excel file. Use this example to learn how to configure the SQL datasource, and map query columns to the Excel output.

Ideal when you need one combined report for analysis, archiving or distribution (email or cloud upload).

This sample shows how to generate individualized Invoice HTML files using a scripted datasource. The sample runs a script that builds master-details invoice data and generates one HTML file per OrderID (naming convention invoice_${OrderID}.html). Use this to learn scripted data preparation, master/detail rendering and per-order generation.

This sample demonstrates how to produce a single HTML Category & Region crosstab using a scripted datasource and the Sample Northwind SQLite database. The supplied script builds a crosstab data structure (categories vs. regions) and the engine renders it to one consolidated file (CategoryRegionCrosstab.html).

Use this example to learn how to: prepare data in a script, and produce a single HTML output suitable for dashboards, exports or web publishing.

This sample shows how to generate a single HTML Monthly Sales Trend report from the Sample Northwind SQLite database using a scripted datasource. The script aggregates monthly sales into a time series and the packaged HTML template renders the trend (MonthlySalesTrend.html).

Use this example to learn scripted data aggregation for time-series reports, and ensure HTML output for lightweight executive summaries or embedded charts.

This sample demonstrates per-supplier HTML Scorecards built with a scripted datasource against the Sample Northwind SQLite database. The script computes KPIs (product counts, pricing, delivery metrics) and the engine generates one file per supplier using the burst token naming pattern (supplier_${burst_token}_scorecard.html).

Use this example to learn per-entity generation, and how to produce mail-merge style outputs suitable for supplier reporting or distribution.

This sample demonstrates ad-hoc report generation using report parameters — no database or file datasource needed. The user fills in parameter values (EmployeeID, FirstName, LastName) via the report parameters form in the UI, and the Groovy script reads them to build a single data row for the XSL-FO template to render as a PDF.

Use this example to learn how to define report parameters with default values and generate one-off documents (certificates, badges, invoices) from form values alone.

This is a ready-to-use Northwind Sales Dashboard — the same dashboard from the Dashboards tutorial. It combines KPI cards, charts, a data table, and a pivot table into a single interactive view powered by the Sample Northwind SQLite database. A Country filter lets you drill down by region.

Click Try It to open the live dashboard in your browser. To build your own, follow the step-by-step tutorial.

This sample demonstrates an interactive Pivot Table powered by DuckDB — the "SQLite for analytics" (learn more). It queries the Northwind data warehouse (~8,000 sales transactions) and lets you drag and drop countries, categories, and quarters to explore revenue from every angle — all aggregation runs server-side in DuckDB for instant results.

Click Try It to open the live pivot table in your browser.
